newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor crowd gathers to await bishop.
newsitem.headline: East Timor crowd gathers to await bishop.

text.p: Thousands of people gathered at Dili's University of East Timor on Friday for a fourth straight day, awaiting the return of Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, witnesses and officials said.

Local deputy police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto told Reuters by telephone from Dili the demonstrators later dispersed but hundreds then boarded more than two dozen privately owned trucks and drove to the airport. They then cruised the city, he said.
"They are being orderly. They went from the University of East Timor to the airport and now they are back going around the city," Rismanto said.
East Timorese are protesting against Indonesian criticism of Belo, who is highly regarded in the mainly Catholic territory.

The bishop, who has been in Jakarta all this week, has come under fire from officials and in the media for reported comments in a German news magazine that Indonesian troops treated East Timorese like "dogs".
He has declined to comment on the interview carried by Der Spiegel until he saw a full transcript and heard a tape of the interview.

Witnesses in Dili said thousands of people had gathered earlier at the university campus to continue protests that started on Tuesday, the fifth anniversary of the killing of at least 50 demonstrators by Indonesian troops in Dili.
Acting university rector Armindo Maia said the people had gathered to welcome Belo back to Dili, but had dispersed from the campus by noon when it became clear he was not coming.
"The situation has cooled down and the people went home around midday. They left after they received information that the bishop was not coming," Maia said by telephone from Dili.

Belo was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace prize last month together with self-exiled East Timorese-born independence activist Jose Ramos Horta. He has been in Jakarta since Monday as an observer at the annual Indonesian Bishops' Conference.
Indonesia occupied the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and later declared it the country's 27th province in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
He said the university, focus of the recent protests, would probably be closed until Tuesday.
"It is really difficult for us to control the situation, and if there is any provocation, we could be blamed," Maia said, adding that Belo was expected back in Dili on Sunday.
"The bishop will come, he will say some words to the people and they will calm down," he said.
Witnesses said police in Dili had so far kept a low profile and police said there had been no arrests.
Indonesian Religious Affairs Minister Tarmizi Taher said in Jakarta on Thursday that the problems surrounding Belo were not religious matters.
"I call on all sides to have cool hearts and calm thoughts when approaching this problem which has caused all this recent commotion," the official Antara news agency quoted him as saying.
